title: Non-Chord Tones
intro: Melodies are not made only of chord notes. Notes outside the chord, non-chord tones, add motion and tension, and each kind is defined by how it is approached and left.

items: Passing tone (P): approached and left by step in the same direction, filling a gap between two chord tones (C–D–E over a C chord).
Neighbour tone (N): steps away from a chord tone and back (E–F–E). Upper or lower.

Suspension (S): a chord tone held (or re-struck) while the harmony changes under it, becoming a dissonance, then resolving down by step. Named by the intervals above the bass: 4–3, 7–6, 9–8, and 2–3 in the bass. It has three parts: preparation (consonant), suspension (dissonant, on a strong beat) and resolution.
Retardation: like a suspension but resolving up (7–8).
Appoggiatura (APP): approached by leap, left by step in the opposite direction, usually accented. Very expressive.
Escape tone (E): approached by step, left by leap in the opposite direction, usually unaccented.
Anticipation (A): a note of the next chord arriving early, then repeated when the chord arrives. Common at cadences.
Pedal point: a sustained note, usually in the bass (tonic or dominant pedal), while harmonies change above it.

widget.title: Non-chord tones (the bass holds the harmony)

examples.label: 4–3 suspension: C held over G, falling to B (then to C major)
Appoggiatura: leap to F, step down to E

blocks.text: Most passing and neighbour tones fall on weak beats. When they land on a strong beat they are accented, and they sound sharper: an accented passing tone is almost an appoggiatura. Suspensions and appoggiaturas are always accented; that is where their expressive weight comes from.

Baroque keyboard music is a catalogue of suspensions: play the opening of Bach's C major Prelude (BWV 846) and listen for the held notes that become dissonant against a new bass. In Romantic music appoggiaturas carry the expression: the 'sigh' of a falling step from a dissonance to its resolution.

blocks.title: Identify
blocks.text: Label the C in each case. (a) Over a G major chord the melody goes B–C–D. (b) A C major chord moves to a G major chord while the melody holds C, which then falls to B.
solution: (a) C is approached and left by step in the same direction: a passing tone.
(b) C is prepared as a consonance in the C chord, becomes a dissonance (a 4th above the bass G) when the harmony changes, and resolves down by step to B, the 3rd: a 4–3 suspension.

blocks.title: Suspension figures
blocks.text: Over a bass note E, the upper voice holds D and then falls to C♯. What is the suspension called?
solution: D is a 7th above E, and C♯ a 6th: a 7–6 suspension.

blocks.text: Sources: Aldwell, E., Schachter, C. & Cadwallader, A. (2019). Harmony and Voice Leading, 5th ed. Cengage; Kostka, S., Payne, D. & Almén, B. (2018). Tonal Harmony, 8th ed. McGraw-Hill; Laitz, S. G. (2016). The Complete Musician, 4th ed. Oxford University Press.
